Vestibulodynia

Two sham-controlled trials found reductions on some provoked pain measures. They did not show clear improvements in sexual function or perceived overall response.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials found reductions on some provoked pain measures. They did not show clear improvements in sexual function or perceived overall response.

Summary of the Evidence

Two independent randomized, sham-controlled trials were identified, enrolling 34 and 30 women with provoked vestibulodynia. The samples and publication dates indicate distinct cohorts; no overlap was identified. The trials assessed different pain measures and used different PBM protocols. Their positive findings are concentrated in local provoked pain, while broader perceptions of improvement and sexual-function outcomes were not consistently different from sham.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 2017 pilot, 18 women received laser and 16 received placebo. At the end of treatment, 78% of the active group and 44% of the placebo group reported clinical pain improvement. That difference was statistically significant, but it was not present across the other outcome measures; at one year, eight treated participants reported lasting improvement (Lev-Sagie et al. 2017).

The 2025 trial randomized 30 participants to real or sham PBM. Compared with sham, real PBM reduced pain more on pressure-pain threshold, the tampon test, and the pain-sensitivity domain of the Vulvar Pain Assessment Questionnaire. The groups did not differ on sexual function, psychological measures, overall perceived improvement, or satisfaction (Antonio et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for provoked vestibulodynia was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell, tissue, or ex-vivo study directly testing this clinical condition was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2017 study used an 820-nm near-infrared diode laser, reported at 32 J/cm², delivered by probe to vestibular points for 12 sessions over six weeks. The 2025 protocol used a class III laser array with 660-nm red visible and 840-nm near-infrared light, progressing exposure over 15 sessions across eight weeks and treating the vestibule, perineum, and sacral region. The broader coverage and dose progression differ from the focal probe protocol; no trial directly compared these approaches.

Interpretation

Both trials found lower pain on at least one pain-specific measure than sham, with the newer study reporting differences on three provoked-pain outcomes. Neither established a corresponding improvement in sexual function or overall perceived response. The results support a short-term pain effect in the studied groups, while larger independent work is needed to determine durability and the outcomes most meaningful to patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term provoked vulvar pain measures Low for perceived global improvement and sexual-function outcomes
Publications and records2 distinct publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small sham-controlled trials found lower pain on some local or provocation-based measures, including a newer trial with quantitative pressure and tampon-test differences. Neither showed a clear gain in sexual function or perceived overall improvement. A larger independent trial with longer follow-up and validated daily-function outcomes would clarify who benefits and whether the pain change persists.
